key_points.point: The authors acknowledge the immense potential of AI to drive economic growth and scientific discovery. They highlight that AI agents can perform tasks that previously required thousands of human workers, significantly boosting productivity. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of using AI to solve complex problems and create abundance. However, the authors caution that this rapid growth is creating an 'economic pandemic' rather than a panacea.
key_points.verbatim: Real output per hour rose at rates not seen since the 1950s, driven by AI agents that don’t sleep, take sick days, or require health insurance.

key_points.point: The document notes that AI has already demonstrated significant productivity gains in white-collar sectors. By replacing human labor with AI agents, companies have expanded margins and increased output. This supports the accelerationist view that AI is a powerful force for efficiency. The authors note, however, that these gains are not being distributed to workers.
key_points.verbatim: The initial wave of layoffs due to human obsolescence began in early 2026, and they did exactly what layoffs are supposed to. Margins expanded, earnings beat, stocks rallied.

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI capabilities have improved at an exponential rate, leading to the displacement of human intelligence. This scaling of capability is the core driver of the economic shifts described. Accelerationists view this scaling as the primary mechanism for future progress. The authors warn that this improvement has created a feedback loop with no natural brake.
key_points.verbatim: AI capabilities improved, companies needed fewer workers, white collar layoffs increased, displaced workers spent less, margin pressure pushed firms to invest more in AI, AI capabilities improved…

key_points.point: The document describes a cycle where corporate profits are reinvested directly into AI compute, further accelerating the technology. This upward spiral of capital and capability is a hallmark of the accelerationist vision for rapid progress. The authors note that this cycle is currently driven by rational individual firm responses. The caveat is that this rational behavior leads to collective catastrophe.
key_points.verbatim: Record-setting corporate profits were funneled right back into AI compute.

key_points.point: The authors observe that AI agents have successfully automated complex, multi-week research and development tasks. This capability allows for the rapid replication of SaaS products and other complex workflows. This supports the accelerationist belief that AI can tackle impossible information problems at scale. The authors note that this has led to a collapse in differentiation among software incumbents.
key_points.verbatim: A competent developer working with Claude Code or Codex could now replicate the core functionality of a mid-market SaaS product in weeks.

key_points.point: The document highlights how AI agents have democratized the ability to build software, effectively lowering the barrier to entry for new competitors. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of making powerful tools accessible. The authors note that this has led to a 'race to the bottom' on pricing, which benefits consumers but disrupts established business models.
key_points.verbatim: Incumbents were in a race to the bottom on pricing - a knife-fight with both each other and with the new crop of upstart challengers that popped up.

key_points.point: The document notes that AI agents are now capable of handling consumer decisions autonomously, effectively optimizing commerce 24/7. This represents the transformation of knowledge into active, helpful assistants. The authors observe that this shift has fundamentally changed how transactions work. The caveat is that this removes the 'friction' that many traditional businesses relied on for revenue.
key_points.verbatim: Commerce stopped being a series of discrete human decisions and became a continuous optimization process, running 24/7 on behalf of every connected consumer.

key_points.point: The authors observe that AI has effectively made intelligence cheap and abundant, replacing expensive human intermediation. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of making genius abundant and free. The authors note that this has destroyed the 'moats' of many companies. The caveat is the resulting economic instability.
key_points.verbatim: Any category where the service provider’s value proposition was ultimately “I will navigate complexity that you find tedious” was disrupted, as the agents found nothing tedious.

key_points.point: The document describes a future where humans act as the 'smart supervisor' for teams of algorithms, managing AI agents rather than performing labor. This aligns with the accelerationist view of AI as a super-assistant. The authors note that this shift is already underway in the workforce. The caveat is the resulting wage compression.
key_points.verbatim: The future of work is less about doing the labor yourself and more about being the smart supervisor for a team of algorithms.

key_points.point: The document notes that AI agents are increasingly using stablecoins and decentralized finance to bypass traditional banking fees, effectively using intelligence to defeat financial scarcity. This demonstrates the accelerationist belief that AI can innovate around resource limitations. The authors note this is a significant threat to traditional financial institutions.
key_points.verbatim: Most settled on using stablecoins via Solana or Ethereum L2s, where settlement was near-instant and the transaction cost was measured in fractions of a penny.

factual_claims.claim: The unemployment rate in June 2028 reached 10.2%, an upside surprise of 0.3%.
The S&P 500 experienced a cumulative drawdown of 38% from its October 2026 highs by June 2028.
Labor's share of US GDP dropped from 64% in 1974 to 56% in 2024, and further to 46% by 2028.
Initial jobless claims surged to 487,000 in Q3 2027, the highest level since April 2020.
The US residential mortgage market is approximately $13 trillion.
The top 10% of earners account for more than 50% of all consumer spending in the United States.
Private credit grew from under $1 trillion in 2015 to over $2.5 trillion by 2026.
Zendesk was taken private in 2022 for $10.2 billion, with a $5 billion direct lending facility.
Federal receipts in early 2028 were running 12% below CBO baseline projections.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: Economic output that is recorded in national statistics but does not circulate through the real economy. It highlights a disconnect between productivity growth and consumer well-being.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document uses 'Ghost GDP' to describe the phenomenon where AI-driven productivity gains appear in national accounts but fail to support the human-centric consumer economy.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This is a novel economic concept introduced to explain the failure of AI productivity to translate into broad economic prosperity.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Ghost GDP is a temporary measurement lag; as AI lowers the cost of goods, the real value of the economy will eventually manifest in higher living standards.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Ghost GDP is a warning sign of systemic economic fragility, where AI-driven productivity gains mask the erosion of the consumer base necessary for economic stability.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Ghost GDP is proof that AI-driven growth is fundamentally extractive, benefiting capital owners while hollowing out the consumer economy that supports the middle class.

unmapped_concepts.suggested_description: A negative feedback loop where AI-driven automation reduces human labor demand, leading to lower consumer spending, which in turn forces companies to invest more in AI to maintain margins, further reducing labor demand.
unmapped_concepts.concept: The document describes this spiral as the primary driver of the 2028 economic crisis, where white-collar workers are displaced, reducing their spending power and destabilizing the consumer economy.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept provides a specific mechanism for the economic disruption caused by AI, distinct from general automation concerns.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: This spiral is a painful but necessary transition phase that will eventually lead to a new, more efficient economic equilibrium once labor is redeployed.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: This spiral is a systemic risk that could lead to irreversible economic collapse if not managed by proactive government intervention.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: This spiral is the inevitable result of a profit-driven AI model that prioritizes cost-cutting over human well-being, requiring a fundamental restructuring of ownership.

unmapped_concepts.concept: The document cites DoorDash and travel booking platforms as examples of businesses whose moats were built on consumer friction, which AI agents effectively dismantled.
unmapped_concepts.reason: This concept explains the specific economic mechanism by which AI disrupts traditional service-based business models.
